title: Frederick Douglass: A Life in Brief
subtitle: Born enslaved. Became the nation's conscience.

beats.caption: Daguerreotype by Samuel J. Miller, about 1847–52
beats.text: Frederick Douglass was born into slavery in Maryland, around the year eighteen eighteen. He never knew his exact birthday.

beats.caption: Engraving from Life and Times of Frederick Douglass, 1882
beats.text: As a boy in Baltimore, he was taught the alphabet by the woman of the house, until her husband forbade it. So Frederick traded bread for reading lessons, and taught himself.

beats.caption: Engraving after a daguerreotype, 1855
beats.text: In eighteen thirty-eight, he escaped to the North and took the name Douglass. Soon he was speaking out against slavery to crowds across the country.

beats.caption: Title page, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845
beats.text: In eighteen forty-five he published his life story. It became a bestseller, and carried his voice across the ocean to Britain.

beats.caption: Carte de visite, Merrill & Crosby, 1860s
beats.text: He started his own newspaper, The North Star, and he stood up for women's right to vote.

beats.caption: Portrait, about 1866, New-York Historical Society
beats.text: In eighteen fifty-two he asked a whole nation a hard question: what is the Fourth of July to a person who is not free?

beats.caption: Carte de visite, Merrill & Crosby, 1860s
beats.text: During the Civil War he helped recruit Black soldiers, and he met President Lincoln to demand equal pay and fair treatment.

beats.caption: Photograph by George K. Warren, about 1879
beats.text: After the war he fought for the right to vote, and served his country as a marshal, an official in Washington, and its representative to Haiti.

beats.caption: With his grandson Joseph, Notman Photo Co., 1890s
beats.text: Frederick Douglass died in eighteen ninety-five, at his home on Cedar Hill. He spent his life asking America to live up to its own words.
